text:
This decision has been appealed to the Iowa District Court [Codycal Inc. vs. Alcoholic Beverages Division of the
Department of Commerce, CVCV008543]
Terry E. Branstad Governor of Iowa
Kim Reynolds Lieutenant Governor
Stephe n Larson Administrator
______________________________________________________________________________
IN RE: :
Codycal, Inc. : Docket No. D-2009-00136
d/b/a Greenbriar Restaurant & Bar : DIA No. 10DOCBL040
5810 Merle Hay Road :
Johnston, Iowa 50131 : ADMINISTRATOR’S
: AMENDED FINAL ORDER
Liquor License LC0020914 :
______________________________________________________________________________
NOW, on this 9th day of February 2011, this matter comes before the Administrator of the
Alcoholic Beverages Division (Division) on the Notice of Appeal filed by Codycal, Inc., d/b/a
Greenbriar Restaurant & Bar (Licensee).
Upon consideration of the information provided by the parties, the finding of fact, conclusion of
law and other information the administrator has affirmed the ALJ order dated October 12, 2010.
PROCEDURAL HISTORY
On April 12, 2010, the Iowa Department of Public Safety (DPS) filed an administrative hearing
complaint against the Licensee alleging that on or about August 25, 2009, an employee of the
Licensee sold or supplied an alcoholic beverage, wine or beer to a person under the legal age, in
violation of Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h).
A hearing on the above captioned matter was held pursuant to the provisions of Iowa Code
chapters 17A and 123 on September 27, 2010. The hearing was held before presiding
administrative law judge (ALJ) Margaret LaMarche of the Department of Inspections and
Appeals. Attorney David Wetsch represented Codycal, Inc. (Licensee), and Assistant Attorney
General John Lundquist represented the DPS.
The ALJ issued a Proposed Decision on October 12, 2010 imposing a civil penalty of $500.00
for a first violation of selling or providing an alcoholic beverage to a patron under the legal age.
The Licensee timely filed a Notice of Appeal of the Proposed Decision to the Administrator of
the Iowa Alcoholic Beverages Division.
In an Order dated October 27, 2010, the Administrator of the Division granted the Licensee’s
request for review and established a schedule for the parties to file objections or exceptions and
present briefs in support of their respective positions. The objections or exceptions and briefs of
the appealing party were due on November 29, 2010, and responsive briefs were due on or
before December 29, 2010. Let the record reflect that all briefs were timely filed by the parties.
A Division of the Department of Commerce | 1 918 SE Hulsizer Road Ankeny, Iowa 50021-3941
PH 515.281.7400 FAX 515.281.7385 TOLL FREE 866.IowaABD WWW.IowaABD.com

BASIS FOR THE APPEAL
The Licensee’s objections and the basis for the appeal are based on that the ALJ erred in
imposing a $500.00 civil penalty for a first violation of Iowa Code
§ 123.49(2)(h). Specifically that the ALJ erred in concluding that the beverage sold or provided
to the underage person as an alcoholic beverage or a nonalcoholic beer and the ALJ erred in
placing the burden of proving compliance with the statute on the Licensee.
FINDINGS OF FACT
1. On August 25, 2009, Johnston Police Officers Tyler Tompkins and Rich Kirkeby conducted
alcohol compliance checks to determine whether liquor licensed establishments would sell an
alcoholic beverage to an underage person. The police department used two confidential
informants. CI #1 who was born on October 11, 1991, and was eighteen years old on August 25,
2009 and a CI #2 was born on May 23, 1990, and was nineteen years old.
2. CIs entered the Greenbriar Restaurant & Bar where as the following action took place. CI #2
ordered and paid for a bottle of Guinness beer without being asked for identification by the
Licensee’s employees. The transaction was witnessed firsthand by Officers Tompkins and
Kirkeby who were located in the same area.
3. In the ALJ Proposed Decision, the ALJ found that the preponderance of the evidence
established the Licensee’s employees sold and served a Guinness beer to CI #2 without
exercising reasonable care to ascertain whether the nineteen-year-old was of the legal drinking
age.
4. In the Proposed Decision, the ALJ acknowledged that the officers neither sampled nor tested
the liquid inside the bottle to verify it contained alcohol.
5. The Licensee does not dispute that Iowa Code § 17A.18(3) provides that “no revocation,
suspension, annulment, or withdrawal” may occur unless the Licensee is “given an opportunity
to show … compliance with all the lawful requirements for holding the license.” Section
17A.18(3) places the burden on the licensee when its license could be revoked, suspended,
annulled or withdrawn.
CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
It is a violation of Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h) to sell, give, or otherwise supply any alcoholic
beverage to a person, knowing or failing to exercise reasonable care to ascertain whether the
person is under legal age, or permit any person, knowing or failing to exercise reasonable care to
ascertain whether the person is under the legal age to consume any alcoholic beverage.
Iowa Code § 123.39(1) provides that the Administrator may suspend, revoke, or impose a civil
penalty against a liquor license for violation of any provision of Iowa Code chapter 123 and the
penalties for violations of § 123.49(2)(h) are set by statute. Pursuant to § 123.50(3)(a), the
mandatory penalty for a first sale-to-minor violation is a $500.00 civil penalty.
2

BASIS FOR DECISION
The Licensee seeks to avoid an administrative penalty by claiming that there is no evidence in
the record to support a finding that CI #2 was actually served an alcoholic beverage. The
Administrator has concluded based on the court records that the argument to be without merit.
The record in the case clearly shows that CI #2 ordered a Guinness while in the Licensee’s
establishment. The order was verified by the firsthand observations of Officers Tompkins and
Kirkeby, the statements of the CIs, and the cash register receipt detailing the sale. Moreover, the
Licensee’s employees made no claim that the bottle of Guinness contained a nonalcoholic beer
when they were confronted on the evening of the compliance check. Based on the evidence
presented, it is reasonable to conclude that the Licensee’s employees sold an alcoholic beverage
(beer) to CI #2 on the evening of August 25, 2009.
Moreover, the Licensee asserts that, because the Licensee’s license was not subject to revocation,
suspension, annulment, or withdrawal, the burden in the case of proof is on DPS. The Licensee’s
license was subject, at most, to a $500.00 civil penalty – not to revocation, suspension,
annulment, or withdrawal. By failing to address the contents of the Guinness bottle served to the
CI, DPS failed to carry the burden of proof. The Administrator observes that argument to also be
without merit. In a contested case hearing, the burden of going forward with the evidence to
establish a violation is on the State, but the burden of proving compliance with the statute shifts
to the licensee. McCrea v. Iowa Department of Transportation, 336 N.W.2d. 427 (Iowa 1983);
Iowa Code § 17A.18(3).
It is a violation of Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h) for a licensee or an employee of the Licensee to
sell, give, or otherwise supply liquor, wine or beer to any person knowing or failing to exercise
reasonable care to ascertain whether the person is under the legal age to consume alcoholic
beverages. The Iowa Supreme Court has recognized that at a minimum, the exercise of
reasonable care to ascertain the age of a person within the meaning of § 123.49(2)(h) requires the
licensee or employee to request identification from a person whose age is unknown and who
appears to be under the legal drinking age. Jim O., Inc. v. City of Cedar Rapids, 587 N.W.2d
476 478 (Iowa 1998). In the case at hand, ascertainment could have been easily overcome
simply by requiring CI #2 to furnish proof of age before serving the Guinness beer. Yet the
Licensee’s employees made no such effort.
The evidence in the case provides overwhelming support for the Administrator to conclude that
the Licensee’s employees sold, served or otherwise provided an alcoholic beverage to a person
under the legal age on August 25, 2009.
ORDER
Based on the information provided by the parties and the Code of Iowa, the Administrator hereby
ADOPTS the Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law, as well as the Decision and Order
proposed by the ALJ.
3

IT IS ORDERED that liquor license number LC0020914, issued to Codycal, Inc., d/b/a
Greenbriar Restaurant & Bar, 5810 Merle Hay Road, Johnston, Iowa, shall pay a civil penalty of
$500.00 for the first violation of Iowa Code § 123.49(2(h). The civil penalty is due and payable
to the “Iowa Alcoholic Beverages Division,” 1918 SE Hulsizer Road, Ankeny, Iowa 50021, on
or before March, 11, 2011. Failure to timely pay the civil penalty shall result in further
administrative proceedings against liquor license number LC0020914.
The parties are hereby notified that pursuant to Iowa Code § 17A.19, this Order constitutes final
agency action for the purpose of Iowa Code chapters 17A and 123. This Order becomes final,
unless a party to the hearing files a Petition for Judicial Review with the Iowa District Court
within 30 days from the date of the Order.
Moreover, the parties are notified that pursuant to Iowa Code § 17A.19(5), the filing of a petition
for judicial review does not automatically stay execution or enforcement of the Division’s action.
The Division may grant a stay on appropriate terms or other temporary remedies during the
pendency of judicial review. If the Division refuses to grant the stay or other temporary
remedies, the court may grant the relief.
DATED this 9th day of February 2011, in Ankeny, Iowa.

STEPHEN LARSON
Administrator

FINDINGS OF FACT
On August 25, 2009, the Johnston Police Department conducted an alcohol
compliance check to determine whether licensed liquor establishments in
Johnston would sell alcohol to an underage person. Two underage males agreed

to participate in the compliance check as confidential informants (CI). CI#1 was
born on October 11, 1991 and was 18 years old on August 25, 2009. CI#2 was
born on May 23, 1990 and was 19 years old. Officer Rich Kirkeby verified their
ages through Iowa Department of Transportation records. The confidential
informants turned over their wallets and other possessions and were only
permitted to carry their valid drivers’ licenses and a $20 bill to purchase
beverages. Office Kirkeby brought the drivers’ licenses of both confidential
informants to the hearing and showed them to the licensee’s attorney and to the
administrative law judge. The driver’s licenses were not submitted as exhibits.
Based on viewing the drivers’ license photographs, the confidential informants
had physical appearances that were generally consistent with their ages.
(Tompkins, Kirkeby testimony; DPS Exhibit 1)
Officer Kirkeby gave the confidential informants instructions for participating in
the undercover compliance check. The confidential informants were told to walk
into each establishment, order an alcoholic beverage, and to produce their
drivers’ licenses if asked for identification. If a sale was made they were told to
pay for the alcoholic beverage and walk out without touching it. Twenty-six
establishments were visited during the compliance check. Six of the twenty-six
establishments sold an alcoholic beverage to one or both informants.
Approximately one week later, both informants provided the Johnston police
department with written statements summarizing the sales. (Kirkeby testimony;
DPS Exhibits 3-4)
On August 26, 2009 at approximately 8:30 p.m., Officer Tompkins and Officer
Kirkeby entered the Greenbriar and sat in a booth that had a view of the bar area.
The confidential informants entered the Greenbriar after the officers and sat at a
table. Officer Tompkins could see the confidential informants from where he
was seated, and Officer Kirkeby turned around from time to time to view the
confidential informants. A waitress approached the confidential informants and
asked them what they wanted to drink. When they asked if there were any wine
specials, the waitress offered to bring them a wine menu. When the waitress
returned to take their order, CI#1 asked for a water, stating that he would
purchase a bottle of wine when the rest of their group arrived. CI #2 ordered a
“Guinness” beer in a bottle.
A second employee, later identified as Katie Cronin, served CI#2 the Guinness
and CI#1 his water. Neither the waitress nor Ms. Cronin asked CI#2 for
identification. Ms. Cronin provided CI#2 with an itemized bill for the

“Guinness,” which was $4.50 plus tax. The confidential informants paid with a
$20 bill, received change, and walked out of the restaurant. (Tompkins; Kirkeby
testimony; DPS Exhibits 1-4)
Officer Tompkins was in a position to see the entire transaction. He did not see
either employee involved with the sale ask CI#2 for identification. When the
officers walked past the table where the confidential informants had been sitting,

CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
Iowa Code section 123.49(2)(h)(2009) provides, in relevant part:
2. A person or club holding a liquor control license or retail
wine or beer permit under this chapter, and the person's or club's
agents or employees, shall not do any of the following:
...
h. Sell, give, or otherwise supply any alcoholic beverage, wine
or beer to any person, knowing or failing to exercise reasonable
care to ascertain whether the person is under legal age, or permit
any person, knowing or failing to exercise reasonable care to

DIA NO: 10DOCBL040
Page 4
ascertain whether the person is under legal age, to consume any
alcoholic beverage, wine, or beer.
The Iowa Code defines "legal age" as twenty-one years of age or more. Iowa
Code section 123.3(19)(2009).
185 IAC 4.8 states that the violation of the Act (Iowa Code chapter 123) by any
employee, agent, or servant of a licensee or permittee shall be deemed to be the
act of the licensee or permittee and shall subject the license to suspension or
revocation.
The burden of going forward with the evidence to establish a violation is on the
party filing the hearing complaint, but the alcoholic beverages division places the
burden of proving compliance with the statute on the licensee. See McCrea v.
Iowa Department of Transportation, 336 NW2d 427 (Iowa 1983); Iowa Code
section 17A.18(3)(2009).
The preponderance of the evidence established that on August 25, 2009, the
licensee’s employees sold and served a Guinness beer to an underage (19 year
old) confidential informant without exercising reasonable care to ascertain
whether the person was under the legal age. Neither the waitress nor the
employee who delivered the beer to the confidential informant asked him for
identification. At hearing, the licensee did not deny that one of its employees
sold and served CI#2 a “Guinness” for $4.50 on August 25, 2009 without first
requesting identification. The only defense offered by the licensee was the
assertion that the state failed to establish that the “Guinness” served to CI#2 was
an alcoholic beverage.
The state has gone forward with sufficient evidence to establish the illegal sale of
a bottle of Guinness beer to CI#2. The licensee offered no evidence to show that
Guinness makes a non-alcoholic beer or to show that the Greenbriar sells a non-
alcoholic Guinness beer. Officer Kirkeby spoke to the licensee’s manager on
August 26, 2009 and to Katie Cronin on August 27, 2009. Neither of them
claimed that the confidential informant had been served a non-alcoholic beer.
Based on this record, it is reasonable to conclude that the licensee’s employees
served and sold an alcoholic beverage (beer) to an underage confidential
informant, in violation of Iowa Code section 123.49(2)(h)(2009).
Iowa Code section 123.50 provides, in relevant part:

123.50 Criminal and civil penalties.
...
3. If any licensee, wine permittee, beer permittee, or employee
of a licensee or permittee is convicted or found in violation of
section 123.49, subsection 2, paragraph "h", the administrator or
local authority shall, in addition to criminal penalties fixed for
violations by this section, assess a civil penalty as follows:
a. A first violation shall subject the licensee or permittee to a
civil penalty in the amount of five hundred dollars. Failure to
pay the civil penalty as ordered under section 123.39 shall result in
automatic suspension of the license or permit for a period of
fourteen days.
Pursuant to Iowa Code sections 123.50(3)(a), the mandatory administrative
sanction for a first offense sale to an underage person is a $500 civil penalty. A
criminal conviction is not a prerequisite to suspension, revocation or imposition
of a civil penalty. Iowa Code section 123.39(1)(c)(2009).
